name: Stalinism
info: Stalinism is the totalitarian means of governing and the Marxist–Leninist policies of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union from 1927 to 1953, built on socialism in one country, forced industrialisation and collectivisation, mass repression and a cult of personality.

facts.thinkers: Joseph Stalin, who developed socialism in one country; Lazar Kaganovich, who reportedly proposed replacing “Long Live Leninism” with “Long Live Stalinism”; Nikolai Bukharin, whose Right Opposition was defeated; Leon Trotsky, its foremost critic, who promoted permanent revolution; Nikita Khrushchev, who denounced it in 1956; Enver Hoxha, whose Hoxhaism kept a version of it in Albania
facts.texts: Stalin’s writings of 1925–26 on socialism in one country; Foundations of Leninism (1924); Economic Problems of Socialism in the USSR (1951); History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks) (1938); Trotsky’s The Stalin School of Falsification and Stalinism and Bolshevism (1937); Khrushchev’s Secret Speech (1956)
facts.ideas: socialism in one country; a proletarian state that grows stronger before it withers away; intensification of class conflict; rapid industrialisation under a planned economy; forced collectivisation of agriculture; the party as the leading vanguard of communist revolution; the cult of personality; ideological orthodoxy in science and the arts
facts.today: De-Stalinization began in the Soviet Union in the 1950s and 1960s, and most communist parties abandoned Stalinism after 1956, except those of the German Democratic Republic and the Socialist Republic of Romania; Albania under Enver Hoxha stayed committed to its brand of Stalinism for decades; historians still dispute whether Stalinism followed from Leninism

t: Stalin developed the doctrine of socialism in one country from December 1924, holding that socialism could be completed in Russia without a spreading world revolution, and used it against Trotsky’s permanent revolution.

The Stalinist state carried out the Great Purge, dekulakisation, the gulag system and mass deportations; Soviet archives show nearly 700,000 executions in 1937 and 1938, and the emergent scholarly consensus is that around 1.5 to 1.7 million died in the gulag system from 1930 to 1953.
Historians disagree on whether Stalinism grew out of Leninism: Richard Pipes called it the natural consequence of Leninism, while Roy Medvedev and Graeme Gill saw a break from it.
dyk: In 1936 Stalin told the journalist Roy W. Howard that the export of revolution was “nonsense”, yet a few years earlier he had turned the Soviet economy from the New Economic Policy to a planned economy in what became known as the Great Turn.
ev: Stalin first develops the idea of socialism in one country, elaborating it in his writings of 1925–26
The Soviet famine of 1930–1933 begins during forced collectivisation, and the Holodomor follows near the end of 1932
The Great Terror begins in September, with Nikolai Yezhov heading the NKVD, and the Moscow Trials run to 1938
The History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks) alters the history of the party and of its leaders
Trotsky is assassinated in Mexico, the last of Stalin’s opponents among the former party leadership
Mass deportations of whole peoples begin, and by 1949 nearly 3.3 million people are deported
Stalin dies on 5 March and de-Stalinization follows
Khrushchev’s Secret Speech condemns Stalin’s cult of personality at the Twentieth Party Congress

sections.origins:
The word Stalinism came into prominence in the mid-1930s, when Lazar Kaganovich reportedly declared: “Let’s replace Long Live Leninism with Long Live Stalinism!” Stalin dismissed this as excessive and as feeding a cult of personality that he thought might later be used against him. The term is used for the period in which Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union as General Secretary of the Central Committee, from 3 April 1922 to his death on 5 March 1953; it is dated from 1927 in the Soviet Union and from 1944 to 1953 in the satellite states. Stalin avoided the term “Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism” but allowed others to use it.

After Lenin’s death Stalin entered the party’s theoretical debates with the idea of “Socialism in One Country”, bound up with factional struggles, above all against Trotsky. He first developed it in December 1924 and elaborated it in his writings of 1925–26. The other Bolshevik leaders had regarded the revolution of 1917 as the start of a world revolution, but it had not spread, and Poland, Finland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia had returned to bourgeois rule. Politburo members from Zinoviev and Kamenev to Rykov, Bukharin and Tomsky at first thought the idea next to blasphemy. It could not be imposed until Stalin came close to being autocratic ruler around 1929, when Trotsky had been exiled and Zinoviev and Kamenev expelled from the party.
sections.ideas:
Stalin’s doctrine held that socialism could be completed in Russia but that its final victory could not be guaranteed, because of the threat of capitalist intervention. He kept the Leninist view that world revolution was still necessary, and the Marxist belief that the state would wither away, but held that the Soviet state would remain until international capitalism was finally defeated. The concept joined Marxist and Leninist ideas with nationalist ideals and served to discredit Trotsky, who promoted “permanent revolution”, as a defeatist. Stalin also argued that the proletarian state had to grow stronger before it could wither away, so that it could defeat counter-revolutionary elements.

At the start of the 1930s Stalin turned away from the mixed economy of the New Economic Policy (NEP) to a planned economy, in what became known as the Great Turn. Industrialisation was officially meant to speed development toward communism, because the Soviet Union lagged behind Western countries, and it came with mass collectivisation of agriculture and rapid urbanisation.

Orthodoxy was enforced in culture and science: socialist realism was imposed on the arts, Einstein’s theory of relativity was denounced as “bourgeois idealism”, and Trofim Lysenko’s pseudoscientific theories were favoured over genetics.
sections.spread:
Stalinism was also the doctrine of the Soviet satellite states between 1944 and 1953, and it subordinated the interests of foreign communist parties to those of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, which it treated as the leading vanguard party of communist revolution. Its methods reached beyond the Soviet Union. Stalin sent a contingent of NKVD operatives to Mongolia and set up a Mongolian version of the NKVD troika, and the Mongolian ruler Khorloogiin Choibalsan closely followed his lead. The Chinese warlord Sheng Shicai, who had Communist leanings, invited Soviet intervention in Xinjiang in the 1930s. Stalinist forces also oversaw purges of anti-Stalinist elements among the Spanish Republican insurgents during the Spanish Civil War, among them the Trotskyist POUM faction and anarchist groups.

After Stalin’s death in 1953 Khrushchev repudiated his policies and condemned his cult of personality in the Secret Speech to the Twentieth Party Congress in 1956. Most communist parties that had adhered to Stalinism, except those of the German Democratic Republic and the Socialist Republic of Romania, abandoned it and adopted Khrushchev’s positions to a greater or lesser degree. The Chinese Communist Party chose to split from the Soviet Union, and Albania, siding with it in the Sino-Soviet split, remained committed, at least in theory, to its brand of Stalinism, Hoxhaism, for decades under Enver Hoxha. He later denounced Mao as a revisionist, along with almost every other self-identified communist organisation, which isolated Albania from the rest of the world.
sections.power:
In the 1930s Stalin consolidated nearly absolute power through a Great Purge of the party, in which those targeted were expelled, banished to the Gulag labour camps or executed after trials by NKVD troikas. After the assassination of the Leningrad party head Sergei Kirov, which Stalin may have orchestrated, investigations and trials widened. The Great Terror of September 1936 to December 1938 was its peak, with Nikolai Yezhov heading the NKVD and quotas of arrests and executions set for each republic. Historians now estimate that nearly 700,000 people were executed in the terror (353,074 in 1937 and 328,612 in 1938), and scholars put the death toll of the Great Purge, with fatalities from imprisonment, at roughly 700,000 to 1.2 million.

Violence against the kulaks accompanied forced collectivisation; several international legislatures have declared it a genocide, and some historians dispute that. Several Western historians count Stalinist agricultural policy a key factor in the Soviet famine of 1930–1933, and some scholars believe the Holodomor, from the end of 1932, was when it became an instrument of genocide; others dispute the intentionality.

From 1941 to 1949 nearly 3.3 million people were deported to Siberia and Central Asia, among them Volga Germans and Chechens; by some estimates up to 43% of the resettled died of disease and malnutrition. By official Soviet estimates more than 14 million people passed through the gulags from 1929 to 1953, and the emergent scholarly consensus is that around 1.5 to 1.7 million died in the system from 1930 to 1953.
sections.critiques:
Trotsky argued in The Stalin School of Falsification that the Stalinist faction routinely distorted political events, and claimed that a “river of blood” separated Stalin’s regime from Lenin’s. Trotskyists held that the Stalinist Soviet Union was neither socialist nor communist but a bureaucratised degenerated workers’ state. Max Shachtman called it bureaucratic collectivism, and Tony Cliff developed a critique of state capitalism. Anarcho-communists criticised the party-state as bureaucratic.

On the economy, Fredric Jameson judged that Stalinism “modernized the Soviet Union”. Robert Conquest disputed this, writing that its industrial advances could have come without collectivisation, famine or terror, and Stephen Kotkin called the case for collectivisation’s necessity “dead wrong”. Michael Ellman held that mass deaths from famine were not a “uniquely Stalinist evil”.

Historians divide on Leninism. Richard Pipes considered Stalinism the natural consequence of Leninism, and Edvard Radzinsky and Stephen Kotkin likewise found continuity; Robert Service wrote that Lenin laid foundations, but that the passage to Stalinism “was not smooth and inevitable”. Roy Medvedev, Isaac Deutscher, Moshe Lewin and Graeme Gill saw a break, Gill adding that there is no agreement on what should constitute Stalinism. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn argued that the term hides the effects of communism as a whole, and David L. Hoffmann argued that many of the state’s practices predated the Soviet regime.
sections.legacy:
In Western historiography Stalin is considered one of the worst and most notorious figures in modern history. Isaac Deutscher stressed the totalitarian character of Stalinism and its suppression of “socialist inspiration”, and several scholars have derided it for fostering anti-intellectual, antisemitic and chauvinistic attitudes in the Soviet Union. Historian David L. Hoffmann sums up the scholars’ consensus that the Stalin cult was a central element of Stalinism and one of the most salient features of Soviet rule.

Khrushchev’s Secret Speech of 1956 set off de-Stalinization and a relative liberalisation within the same political framework, and condemned the deportations, most of which he reversed; the Tatars, Meskhetians and Volga Germans were not allowed to return in large numbers until 1991. After the Sino-Soviet split, Mao Zedong declared Stalin 70% good and 30% bad. Maoists praised him for leading the Soviet Union and defeating fascism in Germany, and criticised his view that class contradictions ended after the basic construction of socialism.

Historians have drawn other comparisons. Dietrich Schwanitz saw in Stalin “a monstrous reincarnation” of Peter the Great, some reviewers have called Stalinism a form of red fascism, and Benito Mussolini saw it as having turned Bolshevism into a Slavic fascism. Seumas Milne wrote in 2002 and 2006 that equating the evils of communism with those of Nazism relativised the unique crimes of Nazism.

summary: Stalinism is the term for the way Joseph Stalin governed the Soviet Union from 1927 to 1953: socialism in one country, forced industrialisation and collectivisation, a cult of personality and a police state. The Great Purge, famines, deportations and the gulags marked it, and historians still dispute how far it followed from Leninism.
references: Sheila Fitzpatrick, Everyday Stalinism: Ordinary Life in Extraordinary Times: Soviet Russia in the 1930s (Oxford University Press, 2000)
J. Arch Getty, Origins of the Great Purges: The Soviet Communist Party Reconsidered, 1933–1938 (Cambridge University Press, 1987)
Robert C. Tucker, Stalin in Power: The Revolution from Above, 1928–1941 (W. W. Norton & Company, 1992)
notes: Start 1924, circa true: the article says Stalin 'first developed the idea in December 1924' but also 'introduced the idea … by the autumn of 1924'; it dates the period of Stalinism from 1927 to 1953. End 1953: the article's period ends with Stalin's death; de-Stalinization is placed in the 1950s and 1960s and Hoxhaism lasted 'for decades'.
The 1930 event is the start of the famine of 1930–1933 as the article gives it; the article does not date collectivization itself. The Holodomor 'started near the end of 1932'.

The article gives the Soviet famine/Holodomor as disputed: Robert Service and 'several Western historians' blame Stalinist agriculture; some scholars dispute intentionality; the Ukrainian government recognizes it as genocide (left out as a present-day state act). Its death toll is not given.
The article gives dekulakization no figures; 'several international legislatures' call it genocide, some historians dispute it.

Deportation estimates are 'by some estimates': 3.3 million 1941–1949, up to 43% died; 'more than a million' of the five highland peoples and the Crimean Tatars; hundreds of thousands may have died en route. Not all used in the text.

Left out: polls on Russian opinion of Stalin (rankings and polls); the Kyrgyz quota example, the 350,000 arrested national contingents and the Mongolian monk figures (17,000 and 100,000 order); Stalin's 357 proscription lists (40,000 condemned); Sheng Shicai's 100,000 victims; the assassinations abroad; the claim that 80–90% of Central Committee members were killed (Rogovin).

The article contradicts itself on Kirov-era detail only lightly: Stalin's 'invented scheme' is stated flatly although the orchestration of the assassination is hedged ('may have'). I kept the hedge and left out the invented scheme.

Texts: Foundations of Leninism (1924) and Economic Problems of Socialism in the USSR (1951) come from the article's primary sources list; the Trotsky pamphlet Stalinism and Bolshevism is dated 1937 by the article ('as early as 1937'); Trotsky's The Stalin School of Falsification has no date in the article.

The article's 'Wheatcroft' passage (archives refute earlier high estimates) and Conquest's claim that Russia was already fourth to fifth among industrial economies before 1914 were left out to fit length.
